title: Three-egg plain omelette
subtitle: French-style rolled omelette
excerpt: The foundational technique: a three-egg omelette cooked in butter in under 2 minutes, rolled and turned onto a plate pale yellow and just set. The fastest benchmark of cooking skill in any kitchen.
sourceNotes: The French plain omelette is described and demonstrated in virtually every classical reference: Elizabeth David, French Provincial Cooking (1960); Julia Child, Mastering the Art of French Cooking (1961); Escoffier, Le Guide Culinaire (1903). The technique is unchanged.

content.text: The plain French omelette is not browned; it should be pale, smooth, and just set. It is made in a hot pan with butter, and the whole process takes under 2 minutes once you have the technique. The pan must be the right size: 24 cm for a 3-egg omelette. Too large and the eggs spread too thin; too small and the omelette cannot be rolled. The recipe is identical each time; the only variable is practice.
Break the eggs into a bowl and beat briskly with a fork until the whites and yolks are fully combined, about 30 seconds. Season with salt and pepper.
Place a 24 cm pan over high heat. When very hot, add the butter. It should foam immediately and begin to turn golden at the edges within 10 to 15 seconds.

Pour in the beaten egg. Let it sit for 5 seconds, then with the back of a fork (or a spatula), stir the eggs in small circular motions across the base of the pan while shaking the pan back and forth with the other hand. Keep stirring and shaking until the eggs have just set into a creamy layer with no liquid remaining.

Tilt the pan to a 45-degree angle. With the fork, fold the third of the omelette closest to the handle up over the middle. Shake the pan so the far edge begins to roll over. Tip the pan further and use the fork to help the omelette roll into a tight log shape, then flip it seam-side down onto a warm plate.
The omelette should be pale yellow, smooth, and just set, without any browning. Eat immediately.

items.cause: Pan too hot or cooked too slowly
items.fix: The omelette should cook so fast there is no time to brown. If browning, reduce heat slightly and work faster next time.

items.symptom: The eggs are still liquid when I try to roll
items.cause: Stirring too vigorously or pan not hot enough
items.fix: The stirring should slow as the eggs set. Let the egg set briefly before attempting to roll.

items.cause: Pan not non-stick or too dry
items.fix: Use a non-stick pan for omelettes. The butter must coat the pan fully before the eggs go in.
Work faster. The whole process from egg to plate should be 90 seconds.

content.text: The plain omelette is a French culinary benchmark. The story goes that the great chefs used it as the test for new kitchen staff: how a cook makes an omelette tells you everything about their technique. A flat, browned omelette indicates a nervous cook who turned the heat too low; a perfect pale cylinder indicates someone who has done it a thousand times. It is the dish that rewards repetition more than almost any other, and the plain version is the foundation for all filled variants: fines herbes, cheese, mushroom, ham.
